entry.title: [darvishnameh] The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today…
entry.summary:
Source: @darvishnameh

The play "Cyrus" is not a return to the past for me; it is looking at today through the mirror of history. In writing this play, rather than seeking to construct a mythical figure of Cyrus, I have thought about a human being who, amid power, violence, and fear, faces a difficult choice: the sword or the word. History, for me, is not a mass of names and conquests; it is the memory of the people who lived in it; people who were afraid, who loved, who betrayed, who stood firm, and who made choices at fateful moments. "Cyrus" is an attempt to hear the silenced voices of these very people; to see the human beings who have sometimes been forgotten behind the great names of history. As a director, too, I have not wanted to reconstruct history; I have wanted to summon it into the present; so that perhaps we may realize that the distance between that era and our era is not as far as we think. "Cyrus" is not the narrative of a conqueror; it is the search for a human being who wants to take power beyond the mere meaning of domination. Perhaps that is why, for me, "Cyrus" is more about the possibility of remaining human in the midst of power than about the past.#نادر_برهانی_مرند@moaser_theater

Demolition of the "Russians' Caravanserai" in Sabzevar: quotes. The historically valuable house "Toumanian," known as the "Russians' Barracks," in Sabzevar was demolished on Wednesday in broad daylight with a loader, sparking widespread protest from cultural heritage activists. Images published on social networks show that a loader on Wednesday, September 18, demolished part of a historical building known as the "Russians' Barracks" in Sabzevar. The "Russians' Barracks" or the "Toumanian" house in Sabzevar, although it was not registered on the national heritage list, had been declared by the Cultural Heritage Organization as a building of historical value. Mojtaba Kavian, Director General of Cultural Heritage and Director of the Sabzevar Historical Fabric Base, said in an interview with Sedaye Miras: This work was demolished without coordination and without permission from Cultural Heritage, and filing a criminal complaint against the demolishers of this historically valuable work is certain.@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] If Taleghani Had Read Hobbes! The late Seyyed Mahmoud Taleghani, in the seven…
entry.summary:
Source: @ahmadzeidabad

If Taleghani Had Read Hobbes!
The late Seyyed Mahmoud Taleghani, in the seven months of his life after the 1979 Revolution, enjoyed a popularity beyond imagination. From his words, the general public sensed a suffering, a sincerity, and a purity in which no selfish personal, factional, or ideological motive had any part. Even those segments of the people who were disgruntled with the revolution and loyal to the monarchical system sincerely held him dear and regarded him as being of a different kind. In truth, the late Taleghani was indeed of a different kind. The resonance of his clear voice in the environment of the University of Tehran acted like the blowing of a pleasant and gentle breeze upon hearts fearful and anxious about the fire of the power-seeking conflicts of the age. His voice was full of a spiritual freshness yet accompanied by much sorrow, warning, and deep concern about the future. It was as if he knew what lay ahead. He knew well many of his peers and the various political organizations of that day, and he knew precisely what goal each of them was pursuing behind their pompous and hollow slogans. He did not enter into the game of any of them, nor did he consent to the elimination and exclusion of any of them. He tried to offer a rule for the coexistence of all of them within a pluralist framework, but it was as if he knew how the story would unfold! He concealed his suffering, sorrow, distress, dissatisfaction, and desperation, but it seemed that the poisonous draught of self-consumption and self-restraint wore down his frail and ailing body and took his life. It was as if, in despair of the notables, he sought hope in the masses of the people. He held an optimism and a pleasant feeling toward the common, nameless, and unheralded people. He regarded them as beings endowed with an innate nature (fitrat), and in his view human nature was fashioned from goodness and virtue. Perhaps for this reason, he considered the delegation of the decision-making system to the masses of the people in the form of various councils to be the only path to political salvation. In his view, consultation, deliberation, and the council were the foundation of prophetic politics. For this reason, he insisted firmly on the establishment of councils at all levels of political and social life. In considering the masses of the people as endowed with innate nature, perhaps his own inclinations were also involved. Or perhaps, in his definition of human nature, he had allowed one side of the human species' disposition to dominate the other side more than it should. Whatever it was, it seemed far too idealistic for Iranian society. Perhaps Mr. Taleghani needed to read Plato through the eyes of Strauss, or Hobbes's Leviathan.
In any case, he was a human being of unparalleled integrity and, in every respect, immaculate, pure, and great—one of those of whom there should be more in the human world, but there are not. May his lofty and long-suffering soul be in the presence of God's grace and mercy at the highest degree of existence. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [yaser_arab57] Work? Get it to the Social and Cultural Deputy of Tehran Municipality. Hello…
entry.summary:
Source: @yaser_arab57

Work? Get it to the Social and Cultural Deputy of Tehran Municipality. Hello and without preamble! We are facing a serious issue in the country called autism and other intellectual and developmental disabilities. An issue that has no single, clear authority and is scattered among various bodies, from education and welfare to other institutions. The result of this scattering, for many families, is nothing but placelessness and lack of planning for their children; children who have no place to be present, play, communicate, and participate socially. In the meantime, neighborhood houses can be one of the closest and most accessible urban capacities for these families. However, families have gone to neighborhood houses, given their numbers, heard promises of a call, and then heard nothing. Sometimes the neighborhood house says: "Autism is specialized and not our job." The answer is that the neighborhood house is not supposed to be a therapist. It is enough for it to be an accessible public space for the neighborhood's families. Sometimes it says: "This issue is not defined in our program." The answer is: isn't the neighborhood house meant to deal with the real problems of the neighborhood's people? Sometimes it says: "Autism is the job of the Welfare Organization." The answer is that an autistic child, before being a file of any institution, is a member of this very neighborhood. And when this close and accessible door is also closed to the family, the result is not just an unanswered call; the family returns to the same wandering and loneliness as before, and the child loses another possibility of being in society. Hasn't the time come for the Social and Cultural Deputy of Tehran Municipality to take the role of neighborhood houses seriously in dealing with this issue? @yaser_arab57

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] What do 23 votes in favor and 3 votes against mean? Sahand Iranmehr. Numbers…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

What do 23 votes in favor and 3 votes against mean? Sahand Iranmehr. Numbers are tantalizing because they evoke a sense of undeniable decisiveness and certainty, but the famous saying "statistics speak" is not entirely true, at least in political analysis. The 23 votes in favor, 3 votes against, and 8 abstentions show that Iran has been left in the minority at the IAEA Board of Governors and a resolution against it has been passed. The meaning of these statistics is that the majority of the Board of Governors has not sided with Iran's position. This fact should not be downplayed, nor should one, for instance, flaunt the negative votes of China, Russia, and Niger to compensate. However, at the same time, this vote does not mean that the matter is over and that new sanctions, this time from the United Nations, are on the way. It is true that the Board of Governors can report the case to the Security Council, but the Security Council has its own specific rules, because now Russia and China, in addition to their negative votes, are permanent members with veto power. Just as Iran being in the minority there was a bitter reality, here in the Security Council, one should not romanticize the negative votes of Moscow, Beijing, and Niger either, considering the veto right. The negative votes of Russia, China, and Niger do not mean that they endorse all of Iran's nuclear policies or consider the differences between Tehran and the Agency to be fabricated. They oppose the politicized process of dealing with Iran's nuclear issue, a path that seeks to drag the case to the Security Council more than it serves the Agency's goals. This is also why China and Russia, despite being in the minority in Vienna, see their minority status fade in New York where the veto power works. If we want to face the issue realistically, we must accept that 23 votes in favor are, in any case, a serious wake-up call, and even if it is proven to be a political move, the essence of the issue does not change. Nevertheless, the West is also far from a complete victory. Taking the case from Vienna to New York is one thing, and obtaining a binding decision in the Security Council is another. The majority formed today in the Board of Governors will not necessarily be repeated in the Security Council, but how far this organized effort based on global consensus will continue, how far the brakes of China and Russia will work, or how far other variables will keep these two aligned with Iran, is something that, in a wise approach, one cannot gamble on too much. @sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] Execution, suicide, and the tormented psyche of society; the costs of…
entry.summary:
Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

Execution, suicide, and the tormented psyche of society; the costs of securitized governance
Soroush Dabbagh - Yesterday, hearing three consecutive pieces of news, I became deeply bitter, and for moments the sky of my eyes turned rainy and tears overwhelmed me. Aida Heidari, the fiancée of Abolfazl Soleimani, one of those who lost their lives in the January protests, ended her life a few days ago. According to the families, Aida and Abolfazl were supposed to marry this very month. Also, Danial Karimi, the father of Amir Mohammad Karimi, one of those who lost their lives in the January protests, ended his life a few days ago. Amir Mohammad Karimi was an athlete and former member of Iran's national youth taekwondo team. In addition, Erfan Mirzaei, a twenty-one-year-old young rapper and singer, and one of those detained during the January protests last year, was executed in Isfahan a few days ago.
Over the past fifteen months, our beloved country has been embroiled in three devastating wars, numerous infrastructures have been destroyed, and several thousand innocent compatriots have been bathed in their own blood. For some time now, a naval siege has been added to the sanctions, placing additional economic pressure on the shoulders of citizens, to the extent that managing daily expenses for millions of Iranians has, according to official statistics published within the country, clearly become an exhausting and distressing ordeal. Moreover, in the January protests last year, several thousand protesting, desperate, and helpless compatriots fell to the ground, bathed in blood, and surrendered their souls to the Creator of life.
Truly, these are strange times. These days, I think a great deal about the dusty and ambiguous tomorrow of our society and country; a stricken society that has endured numerous individual and collective traumas over these same fifteen months...

entry.title: [bamotamem] Scoring in negotiation (from writings eighteen years ago) One of the rules of…
entry.summary:
Source: @bamotamem

Scoring in negotiation (from writings eighteen years ago) One of the rules of giving concessions in a negotiation is that if you give the other party a concession that you thought was valuable and appropriate, and they didn't accept it, or they agreed and then backed out, don't easily give that same concession again later (either give them less, or take more from them, and don't easily go back to the previous agreement). Otherwise, they might not appreciate the concession they receive again. Shopkeepers know this too. For example, when they say they'll give 20% off on something, they give this discount on the condition that the person accepts and buys it right there in the store. But if they say, 'Let me go take a walk and come back,' when they return, either they're told it's sold out, or they say we checked the system and the price is higher, or they say we called the store owner and he said that discount wasn't for this item. It's the same when landing projects. If you tell a client you can do something (at no extra cost) two weeks earlier than the norm, and you see they don't appreciate it and easily pass it by, take a look at your calendar and say, 'I made a mistake.' So they learn to appreciate it when they get a good concession. You might lose out in some places, but in the long run it has many benefits. This rule is followed at all levels of negotiation, from everyday transactions to equations and international relations, and it should be.

entry.title: [yaser_arab57] From a bad school to a good school! ✍ Yaser Arab ✅ We all know that…
entry.summary:
Source: @yaser_arab57

From a bad school to a good school!
✍ Yaser Arab
✅ We all know that teachers' livelihoods are not good. The gap between many teachers' salaries and real living costs and the poverty line is serious and worrying.
✅ The protests, campaigns, and demands being made by teachers these days are understandable, and the demand for a dignified life is undoubtedly their indisputable right.
✅ But the issue of education is not just teachers' livelihoods. Even if all teachers' salaries were increased tomorrow, big questions about schools and education in Iran would still remain.
✅ What should be done with the content of textbooks? What exactly should our children learn, and what do they not learn? What new training and skills do teachers need to face today's world? How is the school managed, and to what extent does our school management structure align with the needs of today's child, family, and society? What is the student's share in school? What is the family's share? And what world is the school supposed to prepare the student for? What is the idea on the ground, and what is the possibility of movement under the current conditions of blockage?
✅ These are issues whose answers cannot be found solely in the government's annual budget. The government may have more or less money. Teachers' salaries may increase or not. But many fundamental issues of education will remain in place. The quality of education, educational content, teacher training and empowerment, school structure, and the relationship between school and children's real lives are issues we must think about independently of the perennial fight over the budget.
✅ This Thursday, September 10 (19 Shahrivar), alongside the demand for "a better livelihood for teachers," we will raise another question more seriously: How can we go from a bad school to a good school?
✅ For this reason, we have decided to hold a meeting with the presence of teachers and those concerned about education; a meeting to listen!
✅ We want to sit together, see the issues more precisely, hear experiences, and think about ways that might improve the state of education in Iran by one step.
✅ We invite all teachers, researchers, education activists, school principals, students, and all those concerned about education to participate in this conversation.
Time: Thursday, 19 Shahrivar 1405 (September 10, 2026), at 4:30 PM
Location: Palestine Street, Italia Street, No. 36, Ensaaf News Base. We look forward to seeing you.
☘@yaser_arab57

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] On the Moscow train, the St. Petersburg to Moscow route was high-speed. Of…
entry.summary:
Source: @ahmadzeidabad

On the Moscow train, the St. Petersburg to Moscow route was high-speed. Of course, its speed never exceeded 199 kilometers per hour. It covered the roughly 800-kilometer distance between the two cities in exactly 4 hours. The route was entirely flat and forested, covered with young trees. Occasionally, a farm would appear in the middle of the forests. The train passed by several small towns and stopped for only one minute at just two or three intermediate stations. The lush green steppes on both sides of the railway reminded me of a scene from Andrei Tarkovsky's film Mirror—the scene where a beautiful, sorrowful woman sits on the trunk of a dry, fallen tree, waiting for her husband to return from the war front. In that scene, when the wind sweeps through the meadow, it seems as if a glimpse of paradise appears on earth. As it happened, the male voice that informed passengers of the status of intermediate stations sounded like Tarkovsky's voice. The man's voice resonated in my ears like the recitation of a poem, as delicate as the murmur of a gentle autumn rain. I said to myself, how could such a seemingly rough alphabet produce words so fluent, delicate, and sweet? Moscow's air temperature was a few degrees higher than St. Petersburg's, but fortunately, it remained at a mild and pleasant level. Upon exiting the old railway station, Stalin's architectural legacy became evident before our eyes. The massive government buildings, known as the Seven Sisters, dominated central Moscow. They were built by Stalin's order to give grandeur to Moscow. From the very first moment of arriving in the capital, the impatience of its residents compared to those of St. Petersburg was apparent! This impatience manifested itself in the ear-splitting honks of some nervous and hasty drivers in the midday traffic. Our hotel was a skyscraper in what seemed to me a protected spot on the northwestern outskirts of Moscow. The security arrangements inside the hotel were also unexpected. A burly Russian man on the verge of old age, whose cold demeanor and icy gaze were no less than Vladimir Putin's own, monitored the passage of guests and their luggage through the electronic gate in the hotel lobby. He seemed to me like a retired KGB officer! Such visible care and surveillance were clearly linked to the war in Ukraine. In St. Petersburg, apart from a sense of ambiguity and concern in the depths of people's eyes, no other trace or sign of the war was visible. In Moscow, however, the security measures at the hotel and on some of the city's peripheral highways cast a shadow over the capital, however faint, revealing the war's presence. Nevertheless, overall, no sense of war-weariness was visible in the daily lives of the citizens. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

The transformation of water from a natural resource into a centralized security commodity has taken the Zionist regime hostage to any disruption (natural, cyber, or military). entry.title: [jalaeipour] I too want an "honorable peace." I truly do. And when I speak of an "honorable…
entry.summary:
Source: @jalaeipour

I too want an "honorable peace." I truly do. And when I speak of an "honorable peace," I don't mean a political slogan. For me, it's very simple: I want a peace in which the people of Iran are not forced to accept every threat and imposition just to survive. An honorable peace means a peace in which a nation is not constantly dragged to the negotiating table under the threat of civilizational destruction, assassination, attacks on infrastructure, and the destruction of its power plants and bridges. A peace that does not mean "either accept our terms, or it's time for the next assassination or attack." "Mowing the lawn" and assassination cannot be the strategy of a lasting peace. A peace built on fear and threat is more like a temporary ceasefire between two rounds of violence. I want peace, but a peace in which Iran can live with security and dignity—not a peace in which one side holds a gun over the other's head and asks it to call that situation "peace." To achieve such a peace, there is no way but deterrence. Deterrence does not mean warmongering; its logic is precisely the opposite: that the cost of war is so clear that no side is tempted to start it. Real peace becomes possible when the other side knows that Iran cannot be forced into submission through threats of assassination, attack, and the destruction of its infrastructure. An honorable peace is a peace without war; but to remain without war, one must also have the capability to prevent war.

entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️New game and new toys ✍🏻 Sahand Iranmehr. This new wave of ethnic content — from conferences, interviews, and articles to posts and tweets — that has surged across social media over the past few days, if traced back to its origins and background, leads to the same group that, before the time of the aggression, had as their refrain "Free Iran," and we saw how the disgrace of their failed "Iran-selling" deal came crashing down, as acknowledged by the parties to the deal. Now, it seems the bargaining for a new deal has secretly begun; with the difference that this time the veil is thinner, and the language is more overt and more ethnicist. Follow any of these threads, and you'll either reach an Israeli outlet or a message from a minister or lawyer attributed to that same ethnicity, who, as before, incites their pawns and followers with the promise of "we will support you"; as if for this final act, they've polished the tambourine and drum anew and tuned a fresh instrument. Before this war, those lovers of the homeland who warned that the "Iran, Iran" chanting of this lot was but diluted yogurt sold as grape syrup, their frothing mouths of insolence would not pause for a moment to brand and shame; but time showed they had neither a passion for Iran nor for Iranians. This time too, neither freedom is their concern, nor even the ethnicity whose self-appointed advocates and spokespeople they claim to be. The issue is something else entirely, and all this theatrical black play, despite all the differences in slogans, guise, roles, and craft in phrasing, if they converge on one point, that point is the destruction of what is the common heritage of us all: Iran. Iran is neither the property of one ethnicity nor the privilege of one group; it is the historic home of peoples whose similarities and differences, side by side for centuries, have forged the meaning of Iran, and any hand that tears this bond apart in the name of ethnicity, language, or religion, before separating another from Iran, has already destroyed a part of Iran itself. Playing with ethnic divides, whatever name it gives itself and whatever flag it raises — if its end result is the weakening of this bond and the ruin of the homeland, as they have shown it to be — is not freedom, but rather the renewed game of the behind-the-scenes homeless with the very foundation of the home and hearth in which all of us Iranians have a share. @sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [jalaeipour] Launch of the "Ravesh" Channel Notes on "Iran" and "Development" For a long…
entry.summary:
Source: @jalaeipour

Launch of the "Ravesh" Channel
Notes on "Iran" and "Development"
For a long time, I intended to occasionally publish notes on "Iran" and "development"—largely influenced by and related to the impactful readings from my student years—in a dedicated space. Topics include defining and explaining "development" across various theories, and consequently the meaning of "social reality," "methodology and ontology," "institution," "power," "freedom," "political stability," "industrial policy," "money and banking," "entrepreneurship," and, more broadly, "capitalism" and its varieties. All that my long—and still ongoing—student years have taught me is that these concepts cannot be understood independently of one another; the key lies in grasping their "interconnectedness."

My entry into the energy issue—today's challenge—comes from this very perspective and stance: "the link between the path to solving the energy problem and the future development of Iran," an Iran that today is squeezed at the crossroads of crises.

In recent days, when I spent part of my time explaining the criticisms directed at my conversation with Dr. Fazeli, the material grew to the length of a detailed article—content focused on the policy framework and problem-solving method. It will be published on this channel in the coming days. Therefore, contrary to my earlier plan, the initial posts on this channel will center on the energy and gasoline issue, and afterward, I will occasionally share notes here on the aforementioned topics.

Yours sincerely,
Mohsen Yazdanpanah
@Ravesh_Analys

entry.title: [VahidOnline] Qalibaf: The rules of the game have changed and the era of proportionate…
entry.summary:
Source: @VahidOnline

Qalibaf: The rules of the game have changed and the era of proportionate response has ended. The Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Majlis), on Monday, September 6, a day after the US attack on several Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, said the era of "proportionate responses" has come to an end. He simultaneously acknowledged the existence of economic problems in the country. Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, in remarks at an open session of the Majlis, threatened: "Any aggression against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, heavier, and more painful response." Qalibaf, who is the Islamic Republic's senior negotiator in post-ceasefire talks with the US, said in another part of his Monday speech: "Severe fluctuations in the currency exchange rate, inflation, unemployment, and market management are fundamental challenges that have put serious pressure on people's livelihoods." He added: "Alongside the military arena, today our main battle is in the arena of production and the livelihood of the people." These remarks come a day after the price of the dollar in Iran's free market rose to near 228,000 tomans, and on the other hand, official statistics also indicate a sharp increase in inflation in recent months. Ali Madanizadeh, Iran's Minister of Economy, also said on Monday that Tehran's reaction to the intensification of US economic pressure is "economic resistance alongside economic reforms," and rejected the view that sanctions will change Iran's course. Referring to statements by senior officials of Donald Trump's administration about the US action to cut Iran's ties with the global economy, he said: "The idea that one can change the decisions of a nation by putting pressure on its economy is a mistake." Iran's Minister of Economy added: "The responsibility for reforming Iran's economy lies with the Iranian government and people, not the US Treasury Department." This comes while the US Treasury Secretary simultaneously announced that the combination of a naval blockade and extensive sanctions has severely limited oil exports and the Islamic Republic of Iran's access to its revenues. Scott Bessent, in an interview with Fox News published on Monday, referring to China's role as the main buyer of Iranian oil, said the naval blockade has prevented new shipments from leaving and estimated that "probably only about 30 million barrels of Iran's crude oil remain that China has not yet purchased." @VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] There is no room left for denial! The Khorasan newspaper, which usually…
entry.summary:
Source: @ahmadzeidabad

There is no room left for denial! The Khorasan newspaper, which usually supports the positions of Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Speaker of the Parliament, in response to Masoud Pezeshkian's explicit references to the problems afflicting society and the country, wrote: "A large part of society, upon hearing these problems—especially from someone responsible for solving them—will surely feel bad about the future. This is exactly the outcome the enemy pursues in its media."

In reality, the story is exactly the opposite! When the president honestly and sincerely raises the problems of society, not only does a large part of society not feel bad, but they actually feel a bit of relief knowing that senior officials are aware of the multitude of problems in their lives and are informed of the dimensions of the issues!

The multitude of problems are too evident and tangible for the people to be ignored or concealed. Therefore, when an official tries to ignore or downplay the issues, society concludes that these people are trapped and imprisoned in their own closed bubble, unaware of what is happening at the societal level, and thus they are out of touch with reality!

For this reason, people feel extremely bad and bitter, thinking to themselves: When these people don't even know what situation we are in and how much we suffer from all these calamities, how can we expect them to solve any problem?

In contrast, when someone in the position of president acknowledges the problems, people say to themselves, at least thank goodness they themselves know what is going on!

The truth is that the era of sweeping garbage under the rug is over. You can sweep a single piece of garbage under the rug to hide it from guests, but a large number of them cannot be hidden. Just as the stench of accumulated trash seeps out from under the rug and exposes the homeowner's concealment, so too does the volume of society's big and small problems.

Those who, for whatever purpose, deny the volume of society's problems or downplay them do not create hope in people but rather fuel their anger and dissatisfaction.

When someone denies an object right before our eyes, the only feeling we get is that they are taking us for a fool! Human beings become provoked and angered when they are assumed to be fools.

#Ahmad_Zeydabadi
@ahmadzeidabad

entry.title:
[sahandiranmehr] ✔️ A dream that returned to die Written by: Sahand Iranmehr
Eurydice had…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️ A dream that returned to die
Written by: Sahand Iranmehr

Eurydice had died once. Orpheus was allowed to bring her back from the underworld; but right at the threshold of freedom, he looked back and lost her forever. Sometimes history's plan for those whose fate is tied to an inevitable death is exactly this: it gives a dead thing a chance to return—not to revive it, but so that its death becomes final this time.

Perhaps "57" was not an absolute end for the monarchy—or whatever other name was later given to it; it was a historical wound whose final fate could still be doubted. But if today some supporters of that dream have pinned their hopes on Israel's attack and its plans for Iran—from partition to nuclear threats, with Trump as a hired hand—to bring it back, and to realize this dream they are forced to stand ever more openly, recklessly, and violently alongside this project, they may, just like Orpheus, realize at the very moment they think they have found a chance at life again that they themselves have sealed the absolute death of the idea of monarchy and kingship in the minds of Iranians.

Then "57" will no longer be just the date of the monarchy's fall; it could become the moment when the idea of monarchy, after a second chance, lost the possibility of return forever.

Orpheus lost Eurydice once more because he looked back right at the brink of her revival. Perhaps some political dreams are like that too: they fail once, but they get a second chance not to return, but to die for good.

Sometimes an idea does not die from its first crushing defeat and blow, but from the way its followers choose to resurrect it.

Artwork description:
"Orpheus and Eurydice," an 1864 oil painting by the British artist Sir Frederic Leighton
@sahandiranmehr

How painful and heartbreaking! These days, whenever I intend to write about any issue, I remember that what comes to my mind about that issue, I have written about it in previous years not once or twice but many times! Two years ago, when war engulfed Lebanon, in this same channel, in a note titled "Waiting for Godot?" I wrote: "The more I scrutinize the statements of the country's official authorities, in the face of a war that has fallen like fire upon Lebanon's harvest, I see no clear plan or strategy. Neither a clear plan for a ceasefire nor a vision for the continuation of the war. It is as if they are sitting waiting to see what happens! Their most important initiative is traveling to Beirut! These trips are not a bad thing from a propaganda standpoint, but which knot do they untie from the affairs of the afflicted people of Lebanon? Israel is practically emptying southern Lebanon of its Shia population and destroying the villages and towns of that region. This event completely disrupts Lebanon's demographic composition and, consequently, the type of political arrangement in that country. This is a danger whose consequences Gebran Bassil, the leader of the Christian party, the Free Patriotic Movement of Lebanon, has also warned about. Instead of empty slogans, officials should seek a way to end the war. Unfortunately, the hardline forces supporting the government have stripped the government of the courage for any diplomatic initiative and only beat the drum of war, without having any realistic assessment of its outcomes. The fate of such sitting on one's hands and waiting for Godot is clearer than to need a warning!" Oh God! How painful and heartbreaking it is that a person clearly sees the outcome of a policy on the horizon and warns of its occurrence with gentle language and reasoning, but those who should see or hear ignore it, and that event occurs in practice in its same ominous form!#احمد_زیدآبادی@ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [VahidOnline] 📝 What do we know about the attack on the wedding ceremony in Sirik?…
entry.summary:
Source: @VahidOnline

📝 What do we know about the attack on the wedding ceremony in Sirik?
🔹Coinciding with US airstrikes on Sirik county on the night of September 1, 2025 (10 Shahrivar 1405), an explosion destroyed a house in Bandar Kohestak where a wedding ceremony was being held. According to published reports, so far five people, including a four-year-old child, have been killed and 65 people injured.
🔹Images from the scene, the sound of multiple explosions in the CCTV video, CENTCOM's statement, and the fact that the attack was not denied by its spokesperson strengthen the attribution of that night's attacks to the US.
🔹Meanwhile, on social media, it was claimed that the house explosion was the result of an "unsuccessful IRGC missile launch"; however, no official report or credible evidence has confirmed this claim so far.
🔹Some accounts have shared old or unrelated videos to prove this claim. The only similar report about an unsuccessful IRGC launch that same night pertains to Khomein in Markazi province and has no connection to Sirik in southern Iran.
🔹Despite evidence pointing to a US attack on Sirik, it is still unclear exactly what projectile struck the house where the wedding was held.
🔹Meanwhile, in the CCTV video, the sound of a drone can be heard, and the bride's father also mentions hearing drones in a video interview; evidence that strengthens the possibility of a simultaneous use of missiles and drones in the operation.
🔹Meanwhile, fragments of a SLAM-ER cruise missile have been seen in the area, but the extent of the house's destruction does not seem consistent with the full detonation of this missile's 360-kilogram warhead.
🔹It is possible that the house was targeted with smaller munitions (for example, a Lucas drone with a warhead of about 18 kilograms), and the SLAM-ER fragments may be related to another strike in the same area (a telecommunications tower about 130 meters away).
👈 Read the fact-check
🌐 @Factnameh

The Supreme Court has upheld the sentence of 12 years, six months, and one day in prison, confiscation of all assets, and a two-year ban from running cafés for Sadegh Saedinia, the manager of the 'Saedinia' chain of cafés. Mizan News Agency, the media arm of the judiciary, announced on Thursday, September 3 (12 Shahrivar 1405) that this sentence was issued due to Saedinia's support for the protests of January 2026 (Dey 1404) and the closure of the union units under this brand. According to the judiciary, Sadegh Saedinia was sentenced to 12 years, six months, and one day in discretionary prison and the confiscation of all his movable and immovable property in favor of the government on charges of 'media and propaganda activity against national security in favor of opposition groups.' The court also sentenced him to a two-year ban from café management after his prison term ends. The judiciary has cited posting protest content on Instagram, supporting calls for protests, closing the cafés and stores of the chain, and encouraging employees to participate in protests as instances of his charges. According to the indictment, Sadegh Saedinia was tried on three charges: 'propaganda or media activity against national security,' 'operational action for groups opposed to the Islamic Republic,' and 'propaganda activity against the regime.'@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [VahidOnline] US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Venezuela's interim President Delcy…
entry.summary:
Source: @VahidOnline

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez signed an oil agreement in Caracas on Wednesday, under which the United States gains majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's oil reserves. This amount represents about one-fifth of Venezuela's vast oil reserves. US President Donald Trump has described the deal as "the biggest oil deal in the history of the world." Under the agreement, the US will have preferential access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields—facilities some of which were previously held by Russian and Chinese companies. Meanwhile, Chevron has also announced a separate $7 billion agreement to develop two other oil fields in the Orinoco Belt. Chevron says this investment could more than double its production in Venezuela within five years. The US Energy Secretary has predicted that Venezuela's oil production will exceed two million barrels per day by the end of this decade—about double the production level in January, when US forces overthrew Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez took power. The agreement has also faced criticism, with detractors accusing Rodríguez's government of surrendering Venezuela's sovereignty over its oil resources. The Venezuelan government, in response, says the deal will help the country harness its energy capacity and attract investment. @VahidHeadline 📡 @VahidOnline

Scott Bessent, the U.S. Treasury Secretary, said in an interview with Newsmax that the United States is not necessarily seeking the collapse of the Islamic Republic of Iran, although internal developments and a popular uprising are possible. He also pointed to the personal risks facing Iran's leaders and military commanders as pressures increase. Bessent dismissed Iran's claims of control over the Strait of Hormuz, saying that with about 17 million barrels of oil passing through yesterday, Iran's control over the strait is meaningless. He also denied reports of mines or two ships hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and accused the media of quickly republishing Iran's false claims. The U.S. Treasury Secretary, noting China's continued purchase of Iranian oil, emphasized that only about 30 million barrels of Iran's oil remain on the water, and these reserves will soon run out. ◼️Condolence message from Dr. #Reza_Soleyman_Heshmat on the passing of Dr. Mohammad Reza Rikhtehgaran
The late Dr. Mohammad Reza Rikhtehgaran was a highly virtuous person with a remarkable inner calm and tranquility. He learned a great deal from the late Professor Seyyed Ahmad Fardid and Professor Davari Ardakani, especially in the fields of art and poetry. He also spent time in India researching ancient texts and the culture of the subcontinent, and upon his return, he took on the teaching of the course on wisdom in Asia and the East at the University of Tehran. He was deeply committed to contemplative thought and the philosophical and wisdom traditions in the history of Eastern and Western philosophy. If he leaned toward one side in matters of belief and politics, he never abandoned fairness and moderation.
One of my unforgettable memories with him—after which I never had the chance to see him again—was when, at the invitation of Dr. Ayatollahi, it was arranged for me to speak on "Paradoxy" in Hafez, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche at the House of Humanities Thinkers, and he was to serve as the discussant. It was a good session. Afterward, he called and expressed his kindness and appreciation. What I remember is that I said the core point, of course in Derrida's terms, goes back to Heidegger's two-fold dialectic and the late Fardid's insights on opposites, but the detailed exposition was my own, and naturally any errors or shortcomings in it were mine.
Once again, I ask God Almighty for forgiveness, mercy, and elevation of rank for the deceased, and for patience and reward for his family, friends, and admirers. Undoubtedly, Iran's academic and scholarly community will always benefit from his written works, God willing.
🖋 Reza Soleyman Heshmat

entry.summary:

The erosion of war and the capacity to think... Once again, American military drones, missiles, and bombs have rained down on the people of the country's southern cities. Alongside material damage, a number of our compatriots have been killed. A wedding ceremony in Kohestak turned into a mourning gathering. In response, Iranian forces also targeted American bases in the Middle East with missiles. Everyone is asking: how long will these clashes continue, and where will they end? The truth is that there is no clear answer to these two questions. The American side holds contradictory positions. On one hand, they emphasize continuing pressure until the collapse of our country's security and economy, and on the other hand, they claim the goal of the pressure is to force the leaders of the Islamic Republic back to the negotiating table! On the Iranian side, despite the constant insistence by responsible officials on the need for social unity and cohesion, no single voice is heard regarding the war. While the leaders of the branches of government declare their goal to be the revival of the agreement and forcing America to implement its provisions, many other voices from within the establishment insist on opposing the agreement, continuing and expanding the war, and the necessity of resorting to preemptive operations. As such, the atmosphere on both sides of the war is ambiguous and unclear. As long as this remains the case, the war will continue intermittently along its current erosive path. The main issue, however, is: to what point can the war of attrition in its current form continue? It is clear that capacities on both sides of the war are limited, and it is impossible to sustain the current conditions even for the next few months. Therefore, it is highly likely that a dramatic event will change the current course. What will be the nature of that event, and in what direction will it shape the fate of the conflict? The nature of an "event" is its chance and accidental occurrence, and it is not predictable. Any prediction in this regard is like shooting an arrow in the dark. Even if such an arrow hits its target, it is by chance and not a sign of the predictor's knowledge and skill! In our culture, these events are called fate and destiny (qaza va qadar), and now our fate is tied to fate and destiny. All we can do is pray that the outcome is good. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] "This caravan of life passes wondrously." Twenty years ago, after completing my…
entry.summary:
Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

"This caravan of life passes wondrously." Twenty years ago, after completing my philosophical studies at the University of Warwick in England, I returned to Tehran and, as a faculty member and assistant professor, began teaching and researching at the "Iranian Institute of Philosophy." During that five-year period, my office was near Dr. Behzad Salki's office. For this reason, on average, we saw each other twice a week; either he would come to my office, or I would go to his, and we would drink tea and talk together. I remember that in our first meetings, we discussed the book "Philosophy of Religion" by John Hick, which had been translated by him and published under the name Behzad Rad. In the 1990s (1370s), when I was a pharmacy student, a few friends interested in philosophical topics and I would read different chapters of Hick's translated book weekly and discuss them. Later, in the 2000s (1380s), we discussed John Hick's "The Fifth Dimension," which had been translated into Persian by Behzad Salki, with several philosophy-researching friends. At that time, I did not know that the translator of both books was the same person, and that Behzad Rad was the pen name of Mr. Behzad Salki. When I mentioned this to Behzad Salki, he laughed and said: "I preferred that at that time, Hick's works, which had just come before the eyes of Persian-speaking philosophy researchers, not be published under my name, because 'the passage of well-being was narrow.'" Dr. Salki was a pleasant, humble, and sincere person, and a tranquility emanated from him. He had nothing to do with anger, jealousy, or harshness, and he enjoyed great mental health. I do not recall him speaking ill of anyone. In our conversations, we talked about the books we were reading and our work and research projects. He was aware of my great fondness for Sepehri and Wittgenstein, and out of kindness, he introduced me to some good Persian and English works in these areas, most of which I read with enthusiasm. He had a close friendship with the esteemed professor Baha' al-Din Khorramshahi. He had interesting memories about the process of translating the book "A History of God" by Karen Armstrong, which had been translated into Persian by Khorramshahi and him, and I delighted in hearing them....👇👇👇 https://www.instagram.com/p/Dcwpaucx867/?igsi=N3k3MHY5bmliZjRn

The dollar price in Iran's open market reached 213,700 tomans, and the dollar remittance rate hit 218,000 tomans. The British pound was also traded at 289,000 tomans. Today's figure marks the fourth consecutive record in four working days. The dollar closed at 206,400 tomans on Saturday, rose to 208,000 on Sunday, and reached 210,000 on Monday. As new records were set in the currency market, the head of the Central Bank said at the 36th Islamic Banking Conference that Iran does not face a currency shortage and that claims of economic collapse are false. In response to American officials' statements about Iran's lack of access to financial resources, Hemmati said: 'These claims are completely baseless. Unfrozen reserves, sustainable resources, and numerous oil and non-oil revenues are available to the Central Bank.' He added that the Central Bank allocated $500 million to the market last week and is now ready to inject up to $2 billion in currency if needed. Today's remarks by Hemmati differ from his previous stance. Last week, in a television interview, he had said: 'Our income from oil sales has dropped to zero; it's a fact that we are not exporting oil.' The shift in tone came after a message from Mojtaba Khamenei, the leader of the Islamic Republic, on the occasion of Government Week. In that message, he said that sometimes honestly expressing weaknesses helps the enemy and emphasized the need to 'explain and narrate Iran's power and strength.' The leader of the Islamic Republic also declared in the same message: 'I firmly state that committing anything that harms social cohesion is forbidden.' @VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

Global shipping monitoring companies say two supertankers carrying Saudi Arabian oil were hit by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other late Monday, August 31, while passing through the Strait of Hormuz. According to Reuters, the Greek maritime security firm Marinex announced on Tuesday, September 1, that the supertanker 'Sider,' carrying Saudi crude oil and flying the Saudi flag, was struck by unknown projectiles at approximately 19:52 GMT on Monday, about 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The maritime security company Vanguard Tech also said the tanker 'Senegal Prosperity,' flying the Liberian flag, was hit by three unknown projectiles minutes later, about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. Earlier, the UK Maritime Trade Operations had reported the attack on this tanker, saying three projectiles struck it as it exited the Strait of Hormuz. According to reports, the crews of both tankers are safe, and both vessels have stopped within a short distance of each other. Data from Kepler shows that each of these tankers had loaded 2 million barrels of Saudi crude oil from the port of Juaymah in the Persian Gulf last week. entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] At 61! Today I turned 61; of course, according to what's written in my ID,…
entry.summary:
Source: @ahmadzeidabad

At 61! Today I turned 61; of course, according to what's written in my ID, otherwise, according to my sisters, I was born in "Kol Kar," meaning the cotton planting season, which falls in April, from late Farvardin to mid Ordibehesht. Honestly, when I look back, I'm quite astonished at my own situation. The factors that came together to bring me from "Qaleh-ye Zardu," where I fell onto the mud floor of a dark, smoky room, to this vague present point—it's been like walking on quicksand. Was everything that happened mere coincidence? One could call it coincidence, especially in this century where not just an individual's life path but the entire universe is considered random, the result of blind forces colliding! Nevertheless, I believe every person assumes some kind of plan or destiny in the course of their life's evolution. Even those who believe in the randomness of existence are tempted, when facing grave dangers or remarkable successes, to seek an interpretation beyond pure chance in their lives. In any case, I have personally experienced something in my life with all my being: whenever, for whatever reason, my head bows from the sky toward the earth, an unpredictable and entirely unplannable event lifts my head upward. I have such faith in this experience that even if, hypothetically, all sciences and philosophies were to conclude that there's nothing up there, it would have the slightest effect on my faith in this experience! Based on my inner and outer experiences, I have accepted that not only is there something up there, but everything ends and culminates there. Hence, the most delightful and sweetest moments of my life have always been when I hold my head high. It's clear that by "up" I don't mean the geographical sense of the word. Up exists in all dimensions of being and in all directions. This too is a way of living in an era that some have perhaps wrongly or exaggeratedly called the age of the eclipse of God!#Ahmad_Zeydabadi @ahmadzeidabad

Last week, to find an answer to the question posed by the esteemed website "Sedanat" about the names of Iranian and non-Iranian thinkers and intellectuals (including philosophers, psychologists, poets, novelists, etc.) who, over the past few decades, have played a role in shaping and consolidating my intellectual and written work, and from whom I have received tangible and palpable influences, I retreated to a corner. I rode on the wings of memories and, to the best of my ability, delved into the labyrinthine fortress of memory, the readings, writings, and lived experiences of the past thirty-five years. It was a nostalgic and soul-nourishing journey. A long-standing companionship and association that has also spilled into my essays, books, and lectures: Abu al-Hasan Kharaqani, Abu Sa'id Abi al-Khayr, Sheikh Shahab al-Din Suhrawardi, Saadi, Rumi, Shams Tabrizi, Hafez of Shiraz, Kant, Kierkegaard, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Jung, Kazantzakis, David Ross, Wittgenstein, Heidegger, Forough Farrokhzad, Abraham Maslow, Albert Camus, Erich Fromm, Ali Shariati, Sohrab Sepehri, Akhavan Sales, Abdolhossein Zarrinkoub, Shamlou, Isaiah Berlin, Gadamer, John Hick, Simin Daneshvar, Dariush Shayegan, Dariush Ashouri, Abdolkarim Soroush, Mojtahed Shabestari, Mostafa Malekian, and Irvin Yalom. https://www.instagram.com/p/DcrMtPfqnIv/?igsi=MzZhZTJiZW9kaXZj

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] "Happy were the times spent with a friend." These days I am traveling in…
entry.summary:
Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

"Happy were the times spent with a friend." These days I am traveling in Europe. Yesterday, I found the opportunity to sit with Mohammad Rahbar at one of the Iranian coffee shops in London, where the scent of Hafez and the city of Shiraz wafts through the air, and we talked for a few hours. It was a valuable meeting; about politics, literature, poetry, reading, and writing... we spoke and listened. Dear Mohammad, in the early days of the forty-day war, he showed admirable courage and integrity by leaving the "Iran International" media outlet; a media outlet that, at least during the twelve-day war and the forty-day war, sadly mixed oil and water, engaged in lies and fabrication, and played a significant role in constructing and reinforcing a narrative that sought to normalize war, as I mentioned in the essay "War, Narrative-Building, and Political Blockage," leaving behind a bitter and shocking anti-patriotic record. Moreover, some Persian-speaking employees of this outlet, during the days when the slingshot of fate rained stones of sedition and missiles rained from the sky onto their compatriots inside the country, leaving them wounded and dead, sat opposite a prime minister who has been called a war criminal by international courts, and with smiles on their lips and body language that reeked of satisfaction and joy, interviewed the main person responsible for the aggression against their country's land and waters, and their disgrace fell from the rooftop for all to see. If I were in the place of those who set about justifying the crime at the Minab school and whitewashing the blatant aggression of Israel and America against their country's soil over the past year, who broke all the pots over the Islamic Republic's head and did not say a harsher word to the enemy of their land and water than a delicate flower, I would melt with embarrassment and feel ashamed. Not to mention that some of these same media figures, using the pure blood of dear young people who were sadly and unjustly spilled on the ground in January of last year as a pretext, made mountains out of molehills without any basis or sufficient evidence, and in their videos fed blatant lies to the helpless, desperate, and oppressed people, earning more audience and making money for themselves: it is fitting that blood surges in the heart of the ruby-colored mourning, for shards are breaking the market of the potter. I am glad that dear Mohammad, despite all the insults and accusations he heard, despite all the arrows of blame fired at him by former colleagues, was not intimidated by the atmosphere; he held his head high, steeled his resolve, and left this organization and media outlet, which, whatever it is, is not national-patriotic, and came to a good end: Two things are the fruit of life: a good name and reward; if you pass beyond these two, all that is on it shall perish. https://www.instagram.com/p/DcoIobjMo54/?igsi=dnp6MzVzajY0djFj

On August 24, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) suspended for an indefinite period the general license known as "G," which since 2014 had permitted certain academic exchanges and the provision of educational services to Iranians. Duolingo, the American company behind the language-learning app whose online English test is accepted by many universities, has now stated on its official support page that the test is not available in Iran or for individuals using Iranian identity documents. Meanwhile, a number of Iranian users on social media have shared images that they say show TOEFL test cancellation messages and the absence of test centers or dates in the ETS registration system (the organizer of the TOEFL exam). Radio Farda cannot independently verify the authenticity or origin of these images. Some candidates have also said that TOEFL tests were being held in Iran until recently, but after OFAC's new decision, cancellation messages were sent to some applicants. As of the time of this report, the institution that administers the TOEFL exam had not issued an official statement about halting the test in Iran. On the institution's website, Iran still appears on the list of countries where the TOEFL iBT test is offered, and contact information specifically for Iranian applicants is also visible. Therefore, it remains unclear what scope the reported restrictions have and whether they are directly caused by OFAC's decision. The general license G, issued by OFAC in March 2014, among other things allowed accredited American universities to have academic exchange programs with Iranian universities and to provide certain educational services to Iranian students.@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] Order to silence! The last time I told someone it would be better to stay…
entry.summary:
Source: @ahmadzeidabad

Order to silence! The last time I told someone it would be better to stay silent instead of speaking was in the middle of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's first presidential term, addressing the late Seyed Ebrahim Nabavi. Of course, I didn't want him to be silent, but rather advised him to focus on satire and not get into serious political issues! Then I thought to myself, where does all this sense of wisdom, or really, my arrogance, come from? Why should I have the right to comment on political issues but Nabavi shouldn't? If he had turned around and told me: Why are you meddling in satirists' affairs for no reason? Sit down and write your serious stuff, how would I have felt? We have the right to criticize and reject others' opinions and ask them to be more careful, studied, and considerate in their expression, but where does the order to silence those whose views we don't like or don't find sound, for whatever reason, come from? I actually wrote this memory and its follow-up in support of the right to free speech of Mohammad Jafar Qaempanah, the vice president. Mr. Qaempanah has expressed an opinion about the importance and value of uranium enrichment in the country that some don't like, but instead of logical criticism, they call on him to be silent! Many also consider these people's own views to be wrong—would they like it if they were ordered to be silent by them? #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

"Happy were those times spent with a friend." These days I am traveling in Europe. Yesterday, I found the opportunity to sit together in one of the Iranian coffee shops in London, where the scent of Hafez and the city of Shiraz wafts through the air, and we talked for a few hours. It was a valuable meeting; about politics, literature, poetry, reading, and writing... We spoke and listened. Dear Mohammad, in the early days of the forty-day war, showed admirable courage and integrity by leaving the "Iran International" media outlet; a media that, at least during the twelve-day war and the forty-day war, sadly mixed oil and water, engaged in lies and fabrication, and played a significant role in constructing and reinforcing a narrative preoccupied with normalizing war, as I mentioned in the essay "War, Narrative-Building, and Political Blockage," leaving behind a bitter and shocking anti-patriotic record. Moreover, some Persian-speaking employees of this media, on days when the slingshot of fate rained stones of sedition and missiles rained from the sky on their compatriots inside the country, wounding and killing them, sat opposite a prime minister who had been called a war criminal by the international court, and with smiles on their lips and body language that reeked of satisfaction and joy, interviewed the main person responsible for the aggression against their country's land and water, and their disgrace fell from the rooftop and was exposed before the eyes of the people. I would have been in the place of those who set out to justify the crime of the Minab school and to whitewash the blatant aggression of Israel and America against their country's soil over the past year, breaking all the pots and pans over the Islamic Republic's head, and not saying a word harsher than a delicate flower against the enemy of their land and water; I would have melted with shame and felt embarrassed. Let alone that some of these same media figures, using as a pretext the pure blood of dear young people who were sadly and unjustly spilled in January of last year, recklessly and without sufficient evidence, turned a few deaths into a mountain of corpses, and in their videos fed blatant lies to the helpless, desperate, and oppressed people, earning money by gaining more audience: it is fitting that blood surges in the heart of ruby-red glass, for broken pottery is selling well in the market. I am glad that dear Mohammad, despite all the insults and slanders he heard, despite all the arrows of blame shot at him by his former colleagues, was not intimidated by the atmosphere; he held his head high, steeled his resolve, and left that organization and media—which, whatever it is, is not national-patriotic—and came to a good end: Two things are the fruit of life: a good name and reward; and if you pass beyond these, all that is on it shall perish. https://www.instagram.com/p/DcoIobjMo54/?igsi=dnp6MzVzajY0djFj

The Path of Return
Iranians abroad who see things differently from what is commonly called the "opposition" come under psychological and media pressure. Artists, in particular, are more exposed to such pressures and negative propaganda. Eventually, a time comes when they prefer returning to their homeland, despite all its problems, over enduring those conditions, and they set their sights on going back to their birthplace. With such a decision, the political atmosphere abroad intensifies against them, and they become the target of the darkest accusations. In fact, part of the opposition seeking the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, on the one hand, treats Iranian artists abroad with utter cruelty and intolerance at the slightest divergence from their own views, and on the other hand, blocks their path back to the homeland and out of that toxic environment with endless insults! Apparently, their goal is for these artists to remain in that foreign land and die of grief! Any artist or any intellectual who does not succumb to this atmosphere and chooses the path of return to their country should be congratulated and welcomed. Living in one's homeland is the natural and God-given right of every Iranian and has nothing to do with the government. Those who deny this right or tarnish its exercise are both cut from the same cloth, standing at the two extremes of the axis of villainy! #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] ✔️Returning to the homeland and fear of a rift in the opposition!…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️Returning to the homeland and fear of a rift in the opposition! ✍🏻Sahand Iranmehr
The return of an Iranian who has not taken up arms against his country, has not called for violence, and has not supported foreign aggression against Iran should, in principle, be a matter of course—not a political concession. If even a modicum of rationality were applied, thousands of compatriots at home who harbor the unavoidable dream of emigration could also stay put.
That the trouble-free return of a handful of compatriots today comes as a surprise to some is the result of conditions that have driven a wedge between the Iranian and his homeland—a wedge that has provided the perfect ecosystem for all kinds of crises to take root and, consequently, for those who profit from them to thrive. So if this fledgling and "still trembling sapling of return" is displeasing to some, it may be because they would rather not see even a single knot in this tangled skein of "Iran's situation" come undone. It is these knots, piled one upon another, that absolve reason from effort, keep the cauldron of rage simmering on its own, and turn blood into a commodity for trade and for garnering support among this lot.
If the fly flees the dunghill, these too abhor conflict and prefer union over separation; because in their view, if a knot is to be untied, it must first receive the blessing of a Homa's shadow, and portraits must dance upon the shoulders of rage and destruction, and a brother must hide a blade in his sleeve aimed at the jugular of his own kin; for in a politics built on elimination, reconciliation and return are sometimes more dangerous than defeat itself, and they stoke the fires of crisis more than ever.
In short, don't be too surprised if they say: "These permissions are meant to create a rift in the opposition!" And don't be astonished if, one distant day, when the Homa's shadow falls upon the nation and the bitter times have passed, this lost lot mourns the dissipation of the opposition and beats their heads in despair!
These returns are, of course, good; even better is when all these differences and even hair-pulling squabbles take place within Iran, under the red line of "Iran." But sit back and watch how, in the days ahead, the knife and cheese—both inside and outside, with seemingly opposing edges—will secretly join hands to stitch the earth to the sky for this trembling, fledgling endeavor. Freeing Iran from its troubles has long since, for some, ceased to be a struggle for change and become a furnace to fan the flames within; and that is how, instead of thinking about solving its problems, they think about keeping them unsolved—and we've seen that if they catch wind of a "Truman Plus" that could wrap things up, they'll cheer for that too.
@sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [bijanabdolkarimi] Civilizational Iranian-Islamic Intellectualism ✍️ Seyyed Mohammad Javad…
entry.summary:
Source: @bijanabdolkarimi

Civilizational Iranian-Islamic Intellectualism ✍️ Seyyed Mohammad Javad Bani Saeed Langeroudi. Intellectualism in Iran after the Islamic Revolution is not merely faced with the issue of critiquing tradition or adapting and localizing new theories; rather, the more fundamental issue is the possibility of the formation of "Iranian-Islamic civilizational intellectualism": an intellectualism that can create a coherent, rational, and path-opening system in the relationship between truth and reality, revelation and reason, identity and progress, heritage and future, and historical belonging and social responsibility. This article, with a conceptual, normative, and civilizational approach, addresses the formulation of the model of the civilizational intellectual. Its main claim is that this model is neither limited to imitating dominant global concepts and theoretical frameworks, nor is it reduced to an uncritical defense of the past and tradition, nor does it see its function as justifying the status quo; rather, it is an epistemic, moral, and social activism that, relying on revelatory sources, demonstrative rationality, the historical experience of Iran and Islam, and a precise understanding of contemporary issues and developments, seeks to produce concepts, theorize, and open the civilizational horizon of society. Civilizational intellectualism is truth-oriented and independent in knowledge; it understands religion as a system with explanatory capacity and social orientation; it reconciles critique and defense, loyalty and reform, and idealism and realism; and it regards critique not merely as negation and denial, but as a prelude to establishment, offering alternatives, and institution-building. Epistemic independence, conscious historical belonging, conceptual production, problem-orientation, foundational critique, responsible presence in the public sphere, the ability to combine rationality and spirituality, and attention to education and institution-building are among the fundamental components of this model. At the end, the article examines the epistemic, educational, and institutional requirements for the realization of such intellectualism. 🔗 Read the full note @bijanabdolkarimi

entry.title: [VahidOnline] The Trump administration has told mediators that it has no desire to return to…
entry.summary:
Source: @VahidOnline

The Trump administration has told mediators that it has no desire to return to the terms of the initial June agreement with the Islamic Republic. This stance has hindered the renewed efforts of Qatar, Oman, and Pakistan to revive talks between Washington and Tehran. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing informed sources, that the Trump administration has repeatedly conveyed this position to mediators. The initial agreement, brokered by Pakistan, sought the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the start of talks on the Islamic Republic's nuclear program, and an end to the war. In return, sanctions relief and Tehran's access to frozen assets were envisioned. According to the Wall Street Journal, Trump has now prioritized economic pressure on the Islamic Republic and is prepared to wait to see the outcome of this policy. Anna Kelly, a White House spokesperson, also said no negotiations with the Islamic Republic are underway or planned, and the naval blockade and "economic exclusion operation" will continue. This report was published as Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, traveled to Tehran earlier this week for talks. Oman's foreign minister has also held discussions with Islamic Republic officials to reach an understanding on the shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar's prime minister also met with Islamic Republic officials in Tehran on Thursday. The Wall Street Journal wrote that the dispute over how to interpret the June agreement and the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz has made it difficult to reach a framework for resuming talks. Meanwhile, Tehran insists on implementing the terms of the previous agreement, while Washington pursues a path of economic pressure. @VahidOOnLine📡 @VahidOnline

The IRGC Intelligence Organization issued a statement on Thursday, warning of escalating social discontent. The statement referenced the failure of "Iran's enemies" in their "attempt to change Iran's government through military attacks," adding: "Opponents of the Islamic Republic are changing their strategy." This military and security body claimed that activating internal crises, psychological warfare, economic pressure, and security operations are key aspects of this shift in approach. In the statement, the IRGC Intelligence Organization warned of rising social discontent and the possibility of street protests, saying opponents of the Islamic Republic have focused on "disrupting stability and reducing national resilience" through "cognitive warfare and generating fear and ambiguity." The organization also announced the identification of what it called a "secret and dedicated structure" of Mossad, Israel's intelligence agency, for exerting pressure from within Iran, claiming this structure operates through contact with opposition groups, carrying out sabotage operations, and employing local agents. The statement claimed that the Islamic Republic has moved beyond a position of merely "responding" to attacks and seeks to increase its role in shaping the course of war and diplomacy. Part of the statement read: "Iran is no longer merely in a position of responding to the other side's attacks" and is moving toward "increasing strategic initiative and influencing the timing, location, and cost of war and diplomacy." The IRGC Intelligence Organization also reiterated Iran's claim of sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, stating that the Islamic Republic's military and "asymmetric" capabilities have been maintained. @VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] ✔️Ali Karimi and Three Thought-Provoking Frames ✍🏻Sahand Iranmehr…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️Ali Karimi and Three Thought-Provoking Frames ✍🏻Sahand Iranmehr
Frame One: Ali Karimi began his so-called political career with insults, and now the very same people who cheered him on are busy insulting him.
Frame Two: A few days ago, I was watching a video of some of those residing in America who call themselves the "Immortal Guard," engaged in so-called military drills in the woods, flaunting their weapons and mocking those who talk about reading books and awareness.
Frame Three: Not long ago, one of these individuals, referring to my novels, commented on a piece I had written: "Go write your novel."
Final Word: In my first novel, "Report of the Last Summer," I wrote through the voice of a character who was once a guerrilla and, decades later, looks back at those memories with a cautionary eye: "We thought we could leave the violence we wielded in the streets at the doorstep and live differently at home." Today's saga of Ali Karimi is one manifestation of a situation that is hardly strange or unpredictable for someone who has read a few books and novels instead of flaunting a weapon or the sharpness of juicy insults. Sometimes, to escape the violence done to oneself, one transfers that very violence to another. To escape humiliation, one humiliates. To avoid being a victim, one creates victims. To avoid being under someone's thumb, one raises one's own hand against another—and when one becomes the initiator of this path, one becomes its victim. Seeing these people and their experiences shows that knowing, reading, and understanding this futile method is no longer a decorative virtue; it is a way to avoid falling into this cycle and not to be surprised when the equation is inverted.
@sahandiranmehr
